article_title: Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review
citation: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137
title: Eight-strategy pattern for overcoming ESL pronunciation challenges within the CLT framework
description: The review proposes a matched set of eight strategies mirroring its eight identified challenges: a pronunciation-oriented curriculum within CLT, inclusion of pronunciation assessment, teacher preparedness through CPD, available pronunciation-integrated training, limited class size with longer class periods, technology-integrated pronunciation practice, availability of resources, and motivation among teachers and students. The review states "Implementing these strategies can significantly enhance the effectiveness of ESL pronunciation teaching in Bangladesh" and that a holistic approach combining them can improve students' communication skills.
requirements: Curriculum integration, regular assessment, targeted teacher training, technology use, and motivation, per the review's holistic approach
constraints: Strategies are proposed for the Bangladeshi secondary ESL context within the CLT framework
examples: The review's Figure 3 pairs each numbered challenge in Figure 2 with a corresponding numbered strategy
key_sources: Md. Abdul Qader, Tanzin Ara Ashraf, Sirajum Monira, Muhammad Asadul Islam & Mir Rumi Mustafizur Rahman. (2024). Challenges of Pronunciation Practices in the ESL Curriculum within the CLT Framework in Bangladesh: A Systematic Review. World Journal of Education, 14(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v14n3p137

article_title: Early Intervention in Reading (EIR)®
citation: Early Intervention in Reading®. (2008). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.earlyinterventioninreading.com
title: Daily supplemental small-group early-reading cycle combining repeated reading, phonemic segmentation, and guided writing
description: The EIR® instructional pattern organizes supplemental early-reading instruction as short daily sessions (15–20 minutes) for the lowest-achieving students, working in groups of five to seven with the classroom teacher. In the studied first-grade implementation, the program ran in three-day cycles: the teacher read a picture book to the whole class, taught intervention students to segment words and blend phonemes, then had students read a story summary with minimal assistance and write one related sentence a day with the teacher's help. Children additionally worked individually (5 minutes) or in pairs (10 minutes) with a trained aide or project assistant, with weekly running records to assess progress.
requirements: A trained aide or project assistant to support individual and paired reading practice
Weekly running records taken by the teacher or aide to assess students' progress
constraints: The WWC-qualifying evidence covers first grade only; the report notes the study took place in one suburban district in a metropolitan area in the Midwest
target_learners: struggling readers in small groups of five to seven
examples: In the Taylor et al. (1991) trial, twelve first-grade teachers were randomly assigned to intervention or comparison, with five or six lowest-scoring students per classroom participating
key_sources: Early Intervention in Reading®. (2008). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.earlyinterventioninreading.com

article_title: Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex
citation: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535250
title: Eight-category content framework for professional development materials on data literacy
description: The materials analysis produced a coding framework for the knowledge and skills addressed by professional development texts on data use. The paper reports that "The content focus categories of the framework were assigned eight superordinate codes: precursor conditions, inquiry process, assessment, data, data analysis, instructional planning, programmatic planning, and understanding research evidence." Each code carries subcodes; for example, the precursor conditions code includes school vision, connection to other initiatives, authority, understanding of the change process, collaboration, focus on equity, cultural proficiency, school culture, and characteristics of professional development. Texts were rated for relative emphasis on each concept using page-coverage values consolidated into high, medium, and low levels.
requirements: The framework would need validation by an external advisory board and comparison to other researchers' frameworks for more rigorous use
constraints: The framework lacks sufficient robustness to support a quantitative comparison of raters
The analyses were initial and exploratory and were not a consumer's guide to professional development programs
target_learners: in-service educators receiving data literacy professional development
target_learning_goals: developing the knowledge and skills of data literacy
examples: Two research associates coded 31 remaining texts with the framework after moderation on the Love et al. (2008) text, and seven text authors confirmed in member checks that concepts and skills had been adequately identified
key_sources: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582807

article_title: The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers
citation: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency
title: Eight key characteristics of strong teacher residency programs
description: The report enumerates eight characteristics shared by high-quality residencies: strong district/university partnerships; coursework tightly integrated with clinical practice; a full-year residency teaching alongside an expert mentor; recruitment of high-ability, diverse candidates to meet district hiring needs; financial support in exchange for a three- to five-year commitment; cohorts placed in teaching schools; expert mentors who co-teach; and ongoing mentoring for graduates. The report states that "the success of residencies requires attention to each of the defining characteristics of the model, and the integrity of their implementation".
requirements: Attention to each defining characteristic and implementation integrity
target_learners: Teacher candidates and the districts that hire them
target_learning_goals: Rigorous preparation for teaching in high-need contexts
examples: SFTR places residents in a small number of teaching academies and provides two years of induction coaching after graduation
key_sources: Guha, R., Hyler, M.E., and Darling-Hammond, L. (2016). The Teacher Residency: An Innovative Model for Preparing Teachers. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-residency

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Eight design principles for effective completion pathways
description: The guide enumerates eight design principles drawn from research and practice: seamlessly connecting academics, career and technical education, professional development, and student supports with K-12 schools, transfer partners, and employers; providing coherent, clearly communicated course sequences and enrolling students quickly in a program; defining student competencies and learning outcomes within and across programs; improving engagement through education and career planning and interactive alerts and messaging; customizing, contextualizing, and differentiating instruction; making academic catch-up a responsibility of all programs using acceleration, modularization, and integrated developmental education; integrating student services with instructional supports and gatekeeper courses; and leveraging technology to broaden, improve, and reduce costs of curricular options and services.
requirements: Curricular redesign such as contextualization requires consideration of assessment, curriculum development, staffing, scheduling, and faculty professional development
constraints: The guide notes contextualization can increase time to completion unless mathematics competencies are reduced to those critical for the technical subject matter, and that technology is not a panacea
target_learners: community college students, including developmental education students and first-generation students
target_learning_goals: program completion, deeper learning, timely progress through gatekeeper and developmental courses
examples: The guide describes three emerging acceleration models: linking developmental and college-level courses, compressing two levels of developmental courses, and mainstreaming developmental students
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment
citation: Dongming Mei, Katherine Moore, and Ben Sayler. (2026). Preparing Students for AI-Powered Materials Discovery: A Workflow-Aligned Framework for AI Literacy, Equity, and Scientific Judgment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09624
title: Eight-week MI module sequence with assignments and compact assessment rubric
description: The paper provides reusable curriculum artifacts: an eight-week module sequence aligned to the materials discovery workflow, three assignments (descriptor benchmarking, leakage and dataset-shift diagnosis, uncertainty-aware active learning), and a compact 0-2 scale rubric. The rubric translates 'workflow-aligned AI literacy for materials discovery' into observable performance indicators across seven competencies from data provenance to ethics and equity awareness.
requirements: Deployable within existing materials science curricula as an upper-division elective module, graduate mini-course, workshop, bootcamp sequence, or cross-institution short course
constraints: Adaptable to local constraints such as credit hours, computing access, student preparation, and available datasets; assignments use public datasets such as Materials Project-derived datasets or OQMD subsets
target_learning_goals: connecting AI outputs to scientific judgment
examples: Assignment B has students 'intentionally construct a naive split that produces inflated performance' then correct it using grouped splits by chemical system

article_title: Redefining personalized learning in the artificial intelligence era: an updated systematic review from 2019 to 2025
citation: Khalifeh, F., Santiago, R., & Palau, R. (2026). Redefining personalized learning in the artificial intelligence era: an updated systematic review from 2019 to 2025. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00440-6
title: Eight core components of AI-supported personalized learning as a socio-technical system
description: The review synthesizes across included studies that AI-supported personalized learning is best understood as a socio-technical system integrating pedagogical design, algorithmic processes, and ethical governance. It identifies eight essential components: "learner profile, data inputs, content model, instructional model, adaptive engine, interface and user controls, personalization goals, and evaluation and governance." This framework organizes how the review defines personalized learning in AI-rich contexts and guides its comparison of related terms.
requirements: All eight components must be addressed for a comprehensive definition of AI-supported personalized learning
constraints: Derived from synthesis of studies published 2019–2025 in nine high-impact educational technology journals
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners using AI-supported learning systems
target_learning_goals: Tailoring content, pacing, and support to individual learner needs, characteristics, and goals
examples: The review used this component set to organize findings across its seven research questions on term definitions and interrelationships
key_sources: Khalifeh, F., Santiago, R., & Palau, R. (2026). Redefining personalized learning in the artificial intelligence era: an updated systematic review from 2019 to 2025. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00440-6

article_title: Generative AI and Student Collaboration: A Scoping Review of Group Work Processes, Outcomes, and Risks
citation: Wei, Y., and Perkins, M. (2026). Generative AI and student collaboration: a scoping review of group work processes, outcomes, and risks. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00217-x
title: Eight-theme analytical framework for GenAI in higher-education group work
description: The review constructs eight recurring themes via reflexive thematic analysis of 18 studies: GenAI reconfigures knowledge development, reshapes higher-order thinking, mediates communication, transforms team interaction, improves administrative efficiency, provides personalised feedback, and raises data privacy/security/transparency and bias/fairness/accuracy concerns. The authors state the themes "can be used as an analytical framework to examine or design collaborative learning (CL) activities involving GenAI" and as predefined categories for future studies. Themes are conceptually integrated and often in tension rather than siloed.
requirements: Studies of GenAI in group work can be coded against the eight themes as predefined categories
constraints: Evidence across themes is uneven; privacy, bias and accuracy concerns are often discussed conceptually rather than examined empirically
target_learners: higher education students working in groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning processes and outcomes in AI-mediated group work
examples: Themes were built through six-stage Braun and Clarke thematic analysis, with codes such as "GenAI facilitates asynchronous interactions" grouped into broader themes
key_sources: Wei, Y., and Perkins, M. (2026). Generative AI and student collaboration: a scoping review of group work processes, outcomes, and risks. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00217-x

article_title: Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher
citation: Mireia Vendrell, Samantha-Kaye Johnston. (2026). Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100572
title: Eight design principles for integrating LLMs while preserving critical thinking
description: The article enumerates eight actionable principles aligned with the six intellectual processes: preserve cognitive friction, scaffold LLMs as thinking partners, embed evaluation as standard practice, activate metacognitive self-regulation, encourage intellectual humility and curiosity, foster epistemic integrity, align assessment with intended cognition, and balance AI-mediated and AI-free phases. Table 2 maps each principle to the processes it supports, e.g., P8 'Develops independent reasoning before using AI, strengthening agency and self-regulation'.
requirements: Principles require deliberate orchestration of pre-AI, during-AI and post-AI learning activities rather than blanket policies
constraints: Scenarios are offered 'not as fixed templates or best practices, but as situated examples intended to provoke adaptation, critique, and redesign'
examples: P1 requires students to formulate hypotheses or generate arguments independently before consulting AI tools

article_title: What Platform Scores Miss: Multidimensional Evaluation of AI Teaching Agents in Medical Education
citation: Zhang Hui, Qu Lihui, Zheng Jianmin, Xiong Yi, Bai Hongbo, Ji Ruiying, Liu Guohui, Chen Wanling, Cheng Zirui, Chen Youbang, Yang Chun-tao. (2026). What Platform Scores Miss: Multidimensional Evaluation of AI Teaching Agents in Medical Education. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/96819
title: Eight-dimension pedagogical evaluation rubric for AI teaching agents
description: The article introduces a transparent, standardized 8-dimension rubric (100 points) designed to assess agent teaching quality rather than student response quality, covering "knowledge accuracy, pedagogical guidance, knowledge coverage, role-play quality, difficulty calibration, medical safety, student engagement, and feedback quality." Weights were assigned on conceptual grounds, with the two core teaching functions at 20 points each and the two supportive dimensions at 5 points each. It was operationalized through LLM scoring under standardized instructions and validated against cross-model agreement and a blinded human expert.
requirements: Scoring by LLM evaluators under standardized instructions with repeated runs, plus human expert calibration on a stratified subset
constraints: Dimension weights were set without formal student or educator input; empirically derived weights are future work
Expert calibration rested on a single expert, precluding expert-to-expert reliability
examples: Applied to 167 student-agent dialogues from 8 agents on the Chaoxing platform, scored 4 times each by 3 LLM evaluators and rescored on 40 dialogues by a medical-education expert

article_title: AI and student motivation: A scoping review
citation: Jiajing Li, Ronnel B. King, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian WY Lee & Ruyi Li. (2026). AI and student motivation: A scoping review. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2672515
title: Eight-type taxonomy of AI education tools in motivation research, with generative AI dominant
description: The review derives an exploratory classification of the AI tools used in the 156 reviewed studies, which "can be broadly classified into eight distinct types based on their core technical features and instructional contexts." The types include generative AI tools, intelligent adaptive educational platforms, subject-specific feedback tools, voice assistants and speech-based AI systems, AI-driven educational games and gamification tools, multimodal AI analytics and recognition tools, learning management systems, and embodied educational robots. Generative AI dominates (n = 76, 48.1%), with chatbots built on large language models the most popular within that category.
requirements: The classification was derived exploratorily from the tools' core technical features and instructional contexts as described in the reviewed studies
constraints: The review states there is no one-size-fits-all taxonomy for educational AI tools
target_learners: elementary through graduate students in AI-supported learning
target_learning_goals: student motivation in AI-supported learning environments
examples: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT accounted for 48.1% of reviewed studies; intelligent adaptive educational platforms appeared 26 times (16.5%)
key_sources: Jiajing Li, Ronnel B. King, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian WY Lee & Ruyi Li. (2026). AI and student motivation: A scoping review. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2672515

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Eight ownership indicators organized into four assessment domains (understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, reflective accountability)
description: The framework retains eight indicators — explanation, verification, reconstruction, challenge, judgment, transfer, defense, and reflection — organized into four domains: understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability. Table 1 pairs each domain with observable evidence and a stated limit of the inference. The author cautions that "the domains and examples are proposed design categories, not a validated scale" and that the grouping is a design proposal, not an empirically established factor structure.
requirements: Evidence and assistance conditions should be aligned with the course outcome and the consequences of the assessment decision
The four domains should not be treated as interchangeable measures that can always compensate for one another
constraints: A short assignment may sample only two domains, whereas a capstone may require broader coverage
Repetition of a familiar account may not establish adaptable understanding; one task does not establish broad competence or long-term retention
target_learning_goals: demonstrating understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability in assessed work
examples: For a policy analysis, the student might reconstruct the connection between an intervention, its assumptions, and the expected outcome; for a programming task, trace how a central function handles a problematic input
key_sources: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957

article_title: Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 717–741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9
title: Eight generative learning strategies: summarizing, mapping, drawing, imagining, self-testing, self-explaining, teaching, and enacting
description: The article's central organizing taxonomy is a set of eight learning strategies "intended to promote generative learning." The set spans verbal-summative strategies (summarizing), visual-structural strategies (mapping, drawing), imagery strategies (imagining), verification strategies (self-testing), elaboration strategies (self-explaining), social strategies (teaching), and embodied strategies (enacting). Each strategy is treated in the review with a description, exemplary research, boundary conditions, and implementation recommendations.
requirements: Each strategy must be implemented so that learners generate cognitive products that reorganize and integrate material with prior knowledge
target_learners: Students learning expository or instructional material across age levels
target_learning_goals: Generative processing leading to understanding and transfer
examples: The abstract enumerates the eight strategies: "summarizing, mapping, drawing, imagining, self-testing, self-explaining, teaching, and enacting."

article_title: Do Experiences With Nature Promote Learning? Converging Evidence of a Cause-and-Effect Relationship
citation: Kuo M, Barnes M and Jordan C (2019) Do Experiences With Nature Promote Learning? Converging Evidence of a Cause-and-Effect Relationship. Front. Psychol. 10:305. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00305
title: Eight-pathway framework linking nature experiences to learning and development
description: The review proposes a framework (Figure 1) in which experiences with nature promote academic learning, personal development, and environmental stewardship via at least eight distinct pathways: five centered in the learner (rejuvenated attention, stress relief, self-discipline, motivation and enjoyment, physical activity and fitness) and three in the learning context (calmer, quieter, safer settings; warmer, more cooperative relations; loose parts plus autonomy fostering beneficial play). The review states that "at least eight distinct pathways plausibly contribute to these outcomes" and that the multiplicity of mechanisms may explain the consistency of the nature-learning relationship. Relationships with experimental support are marked with an asterisk in the figure; qualified causal language is used elsewhere.
requirements: Evidence for each pathway must be distinguished between experimental cause-and-effect evidence and merely converging associational evidence, as the review does
constraints: The review uses qualified causal language (e.g., "seems to increase") where converging but non-experimental evidence points to a likely causal relationship; loose-parts play effects on child development have yet to be quantitatively demonstrated
target_learners: children and students in formal and informal educational settings
examples: The review maps exposures (e.g., classroom views of trees, school gardens, field trips), mechanisms, and outcomes in Figure 1, marking experimentally supported links such as nature boosting concentration and retention of subject matter
key_sources: Kuo M, Barnes M and Jordan C (2019) Do Experiences With Nature Promote Learning? Converging Evidence of a Cause-and-Effect Relationship. Front. Psychol. 10:305. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00305

article_title: Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature
citation: Briesch, A.M., Daniels, B. & Beneville, M. (2019). Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature. J Behav Educ 28, 54–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-018-9303-1
title: Taxonomy of eight primary self-management intervention configurations used in school-based single-case research
description: The review organizes the school-based self-management literature by the specific intervention configuration employed, distinguishing approaches such as prompted self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement based on both accuracy and performance, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing. The authors state that "eight primary approaches to self-management were utilized across more than one study" within the 56 studies reviewed. This taxonomy provides the organizing framework for evaluating component-level effectiveness.
requirements: Interventions must be describable by their specific component configuration (e.g., prompting, reinforcement, graphing) to be classified within the taxonomy.
constraints: Derived from single-case design studies in school-based literature only.
target_learners: K-12 students with behavioral needs, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Improved classroom behavior such as on-task behavior and reduced disruptive or off-task behavior
examples: The review classified 56 single-case studies and found prompted self-monitoring in 23 of them, self-monitoring plus reinforcement in 6, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing in 5.
key_sources: Briesch, A.M., Daniels, B. & Beneville, M. (2019). Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature. J Behav Educ 28, 54–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-018-9303-1

article_title: The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Francis, D. A.; Caruana, N.; Hudson, J. L.; McArthur, G. M. (2019). The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2018.09.002
title: Eight-moderator framework for explaining inconsistent findings on poor reading and internalising problems
description: The article proposes eight potential moderators that may explain inconsistent findings across studies of poor reading and internalising problems: "anxiety disorder subtype", poor reading subtype, attention, sex, age, ethnicity, type of informant, and type of internalising measure (clinical interview versus questionnaire). The framework treats mixed results across studies as a red flag for heterogeneity, suggesting only a subgroup of poor readers may have internalising problems. It organises the review's second aim of evaluating theoretical and methodological moderators of the association.
requirements: Subgroup analyses require 10 or more studies per moderator to yield reliable comparisons of effect sizes, as the article states for its planned analyses.
constraints: The review could not test any of the eight moderators meta-analytically because there were fewer than 10 studies per subgroup; moderator evidence was only narratively synthesised.
target_learners: poor readers aged 6 to 12 years, adolescents aged 13 to 18 years, and adults aged 18+ years
target_learning_goals: understanding emotional risk (anxiety and depression) associated with poor reading
examples: The review coded studies into subgroups such as five anxiety disorder subtypes, four poor reading subtypes, and four informant types before finding the subgroups underpowered.
key_sources: Francis, D. A.; Caruana, N.; Hudson, J. L.; McArthur, G. M. (2019). The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2018.09.002

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Eight interrelated systemic factors determine the effectiveness of graduate attribute achievement, with assessment one among them
description: The paper proposes that graduate attribute achievement depends on eight systemic factors identified by the National Graduate Attributes Project: 'Conceptualisation, Stakeholders, Implementation strategy, Curriculum approach, Assessment, Staff development, Quality assurance, Student-centredness'. The factors were found to interact with and influence each other, so the other seven factors shape assessment practice and add systemic complexity. The paper argues assessment of graduate attributes is 'unlikely to be resolved unless these factors are addressed at a systemic level'.
requirements: Institutional change must address all eight factors together rather than assessment in isolation
constraints: Factors were identified from a study of Australian universities; influence of specific stakeholder groups varies between university types and award programmes
target_learning_goals: graduate attributes such as critical thinking, communication and lifelong learning
examples: The National GAP study investigated Australian universities' efforts to achieve graduate attributes and confirmed assessment as a key determinant of implementation effectiveness
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: EISEL: web-based learning tool with question pools, immediate feedback, and repetition
description: EISEL is a learning tool within the in-house LMS used in the study. It presents sets of five questions at a time from chapter-based pools (e.g., 38 questions for chapter 1, 112 for chapter 2), shows correct/wrong answers with green/red buttons, and allows students to request new random sets. Students do a minimum of 20 questions, can practice in groups, and develop their own strategies; the objective is engagement with domain content rather than assessment.
requirements: Students are asked to do a minimum of 20 questions but encouraged to do as many as they feel necessary
constraints: Question pools are limited per chapter, varying by chapter
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory MIS and information technology courses
target_learning_goals: engaging students in processing domain content through repeated practice with immediate feedback

article_title: Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation
citation: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation.
title: Eight-dimension pre/post essay rubric for literary argumentation and interpretation
description: The study assessed individual learning with a written compare/contrast essay task administered before and after the module, counterbalanced across two story sets. The article states "Essays were evaluated on eight dimensions that reflect aspects of argumentation and interpretation in the literary domain": claims, evidence, and reasoning; substance of claim, symbolic interpretation, thematic interpretation, and synthesis through comparison/contrast; plus organization. Score points were set when the intraclass correlation coefficient for a dimension reached at least .80.
requirements: Rubric development based on a broad sample of approximately 200 essays from grades 6–12
Blind scoring of pre and post essays at the same time
constraints: Stories at pre and post were not part of the module and were anticipated to be highly challenging for ninth graders before instruction
target_learners: adolescent students in grades 6–12 English Language Arts
examples: The first two authors scored all essays, reaching 88% agreement on score point assignments, with a third scorer reaching 84% agreement on six randomly selected essays.

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Eight controversies framing the future direction of the CSCL field
description: Wise and Schwarz's review distills "eight controversies in the field" from written interviews with CSCL experts, written as debates between a provocateur and a conciliator and viewed as "narrative reviews of the field." The eight provocations range from tool frameworks and learner agency versus collaborative scripting, through collaboration ideology and co-alienation of analytical and interpretive approaches, to computational approaches, learning analytics, evolving or becoming irrelevant, and giving up on educational change.
requirements: The controversies rest on a synthesis of review studies and written interviews with CSCL experts, plus the authors' own work in the field.
constraints: The paper is written in an unconventional argumentative-dialogue genre, and its positions are provocations rather than settled conclusions.
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning-sciences community
target_learning_goals: Framing unresolved foundational debates about collaborative learning research and design
examples: Provocations include 'The blossoming of CSCL tools necessitates "one framework to rule them all"' and 'Prioritize learner agency over collaborative scripting.'

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Normative five-step model of evidence-informed reasoning about classroom situations
description: The article adopts a normative model of EIR skills (attributed to Greisel et al., 2022) in which optimal evidence-informed reasoning about classroom situations proceeds through five steps: "problem identification", "problem description", "problem explanation", "goal setting", and "select actions". The teacher first identifies a problem requiring attention, describes it, explains it by reconstructing causal relationships under consideration of scientific evidence, formulates a desired goal state, and selects an action likely to reach that goal. The study uses this model both to structure the case-analysis task and to score EIR recognition and application skills.
requirements: Learners need declarative knowledge of the five steps, e.g. via explicit teaching and an example of the five steps available throughout the task
constraints: The article focuses only on the first two skill-acquisition phases (declarative and procedural knowledge), since the fine-tuning phase extends beyond pre-service teacher education
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed reasoning about authentic classroom situations
examples: Participants analyzed a case vignette with six problems using the five steps, with an example of the steps available throughout the peer-feedback process
key_sources: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4

citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Skill-acquisition account: EIR skills develop from declarative knowledge (recognition) to procedural knowledge (application)
description: The article frames EIR skill acquisition with a three-phase account drawn from skill acquisition research (citing Anderson & Lebiere, 1998; Wecker & Fischer, 2014): learners first acquire declarative knowledge that helps them reproduce and identify instances of the skill (measured as EIR recognition skills), then convert it into procedural knowledge through practice (measured as EIR application skills), and finally fine-tune it through extensive application. The study targets only the first two phases and uses this account to justify teaching the steps explicitly, providing practice with authentic cases, and scaffolding during proceduralization.
requirements: Explicit teaching of the reasoning steps, opportunities to practice application on authentic classroom cases, and scaffolding during the proceduralization phase
constraints: The third phase (fine-tuning through extensive practice) extends beyond pre-service teacher education and is not addressed
examples: The posttest measured recognition via ranking analyses by quality and application via coding an unguided case analysis one week later

article_title: Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation
citation: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. Review of Educational Research. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leveraging+What+Students+Know+to+Make+Sense+of+Texts+Prior+Knowledge+Activation
title: Eight-category taxonomy of prior knowledge activation techniques
description: The review inductively grouped 30 unique activation techniques into eight categories: "open-ended prompts, procedural or strategic supports during reading, visual representation, analogical reasoning, text alteration, augmented activation, extra-textual activities, and spontaneous activation." Categories were derived from shared attributes such as mode of activation (e.g., questioning, altering the text), with no explicit hierarchy; some techniques belonged to more than one category. Open-ended prompts were the largest category, investigated in 23 of 54 articles, while spontaneous activation has the least empirical evidence and requires less explicit prompting.
requirements: Techniques must involve an explicit, intended activation of students' prior knowledge during a connected-text learning task to fall within the taxonomy's scope
constraints: Derived from 54 peer-reviewed articles on K-16 text-based learning, mostly expository texts, so narrative-text activation is underrepresented
target_learners: K-16 students reading connected expository or narrative texts
target_learning_goals: Text comprehension and learning from text
examples: The review describes visual representations as concept maps helping students see relations between concepts and sub-concepts, and text alteration as manipulating texts so a known concept (e.g., tire pressure) supports learning a new one (e.g., wind flow patterns)

article_title: The effect of practice upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension.
citation: Whipple, G. M. (1910). The effect of practise upon the range of visual attention and of visual apprehension. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com/books?q=Whipple+effect+of+practise+range+of+visual+attention+apprehension
title: Eight-factor account of the conditions determining efficiency in quick visual apprehension
description: From a qualitative analysis of the apprehension data, the article proposes that efficiency in visual apprehension is conditioned upon eight factors: native capacity, degree of attention, type of material, ease of assimilation, obstruction or distraction, ideational type, voluntary restriction, and grouping. The article states that "apprehension is greatly facilitated by any scheme that permits of grouping the constituent elements in the field," calling grouping perhaps the most important single factor in practise-improvement after habituation.
requirements: Performance must be scored per material type (dots, pictures, drawings, nonsense syllables, poetry, objects) for the factors to be distinguished
constraints: The article states native capacity was believed unaffected by practise
The account derives from a qualitative analysis of three adult observers, not a quantitative test of the factors
target_learners: adult observers in laboratory perception tasks
target_learning_goals: quick visual perception and attentive observation
examples: Observers arbitrarily rearranged irregular dot groups into two to four groups of three to six dots, and split drawings into components recombined by analysis and synthesis

article_title: Individual differences in addition strategy choice: A psychometric evaluation.
citation: Rhodes, K. T., Lukowski, S., Branum-Martin, L., Opfer, J., Geary, D. C., & Petrill, S. A. (2018). Individual Differences in Addition Strategy Choice: A Psychometric Evaluation. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11360214/
title: Explanatory Item Response Theory (EIRT) as a psychometric framework for jointly estimating item and person effects on problem solving
description: EIRT is described as "a special name given to models of multilevel, categorical responses, in which latent estimates are generated for both item and person parameters and explanatory variables can be modeled as predictors of responses across levels of analysis". It combines experimental design with observational measurement to yield explanatory measurement. The article maps SCM postulates onto crossclassified, mixed-effects, and bivariate EIRT specifications, using random intercepts and slopes for items and persons in adolescent addition data.
requirements: Responses must be crossclassified in items and persons; models are estimated with Bayesian methods (Mplus 7 in this study)
constraints: Mplus 7 does not allow estimation of categorical outcome residual variance at the within level of crossclassified models
Twin dyadic clustering could not be modeled, so twin pairs were split into random singletons
examples: Applied to 376 adolescents solving 30 addition problems with interview-coded strategies and bivariate solution time and accuracy outcomes

article_title: Language-independent and language-specific aspects of early literacy: An evaluation of the common underlying proficiency model.
citation: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179
title: Evidence-based instruction in either language should build code-related skills in both languages for language-minority preschoolers, but language instruction benefits only the language of instruction
description: Because code-related skills showed a common underlying proficiency, the authors argue "the presence of language-independent early literacy skills suggests that instruction in L1 will improve code-related skills in both L1 and L2." For oral language, however, "beneficial effects of language exposure and instruction will only be seen in the language of instruction." Educators can therefore choose either language for code-related foundations but must target each language separately for vocabulary and language skills.
requirements: Instruction should be evidence-based; the common underlying proficiency applies to code-related skills, not oral language
constraints: The authors caution results should be interpreted with caution, noting some studies of older children find L1 vocabulary uniquely predicts L2 reading comprehension, contrasting with this pattern
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness, print knowledge, and oral language development
examples: The study found code-related skills of language-minority children approximately equivalent to monolingual peers despite lower language skills, a pattern the authors say this explains
key_sources: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179

article_title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
citation: Michael J. Parker, Caitlin Anderson, Claire Stone, YeaRim Oh. (2024). A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00414-0
title: Eight-tag course feedback classification system suitable for varied course types and amenable to customization
description: A set of eight generalizable tags (course logistics and fit, curriculum, teaching modality, teaching, assessment, resources, peer and teacher interaction, other) developed by the authors for multi-label classification of open-ended course feedback. Each tag carries "A one to three sentence description of each tag" so humans or LLMs can apply it, and the same descriptions served as LLM prompt context. The set was reduced from 71 initial labels after low inter-rater agreement, then iteratively tested on sets of 100 responses.
requirements: Tag descriptions must be adapted or kept current so tags can be applied appropriately by annotators or prompts; the intent is that others can adapt the tags by modifying the description portion for their own purposes.
constraints: Developed and validated on online biomedical science course feedback; the article presents it as also intended for other educational offerings but reports testing on this program's data.
target_learners: higher education / online biomedical science course students (whose feedback the tags classify)
target_learning_goals: analysis of student feedback to guide course improvement and quality assurance
examples: Four authors independently labeled 2,500 survey responses with the final tag set; inter-rater agreement was evaluated with Jaccard similarity averaged across rater pairs.

citation: Sun, C., Major, L., Daltry, R., Obradovic, L., & Friedberg, A. (2026). Enhancing literacy and numeracy through teacher dashboards and digital personalised learning: an A/B/C test in Kenyan early years education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10703-1
title: EIDU DPL tool with LSTM-based personalised learning sequence
description: The study was built on an existing DPL tool developed by EIDU, 'pre-installed as an application on low-cost Android devices purchasable for less than $50'. The tool offers learner-facing content aligned to the Kenyan national curriculum, structured by literacy and numeracy domains covering 25 literacy and 23 numeracy substrands across 2,239 units. 'The sequence of these learning units is personalised to support each learner's progression using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network', which functions offline to mitigate low-connectivity issues.
requirements: Learners interact with a collection of learning units personalised to their predicted current competency level, with teachers able to align digital content with classroom teaching by selecting specific substrands.
constraints: The algorithm functions offline to mitigate low-connectivity issues, and the intended usage time is 5 minutes per session using up to two devices shared per class.

article_title: Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework
citation: Thomas K. F. Chiu, Murat Çoban, Ismaila Temitayo Sanusi, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale. (2025). Validating student AI competency self-efficacy (SAICS) scale and its framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10512-y
title: Eight-dimension AI competency framework for K-12 students grounded in teacher perspectives
description: The framework defines student AI competency as the capacity "to use AI to support their learning ethically, healthily, and productively" across eight dimensions: Interdisciplinary Learning with AI (ILAI), Assessment with AI (ASAI), Decision Making with AI (DMAI), Data, Ethics, and AI (DEAI), Designing AI (DGAI), Multimedia Creation with AI (MCAI), Human-Centric Learning (HCLG), and Confidence with AI (CFAI). It was derived from teacher panelists via Delphi consensus and extends UNESCO's four-component framework by adding learning-activity dimensions such as interdisciplinary learning, assessment, and multimedia creation. Each dimension is elaborated with example competencies, e.g., judging AI-generated essays (DMAI) and protecting personal data (DEAI).
requirements: Delphi panel of experienced K-12 AI education professionals to establish dimension consensus
constraints: The article states the framework "focuses mostly on the level of AI competency" and does not incorporate data, mathematics, science, and computation literacies
target_learners: K-12 students (grades 7–12 in the validation sample)
target_learning_goals: student AI competency: using AI ethically, safely, healthily, and productively in learning
examples: The Delphi panel renamed dimensions such as changing "Support for learning" to "Interdisciplinary learning with AI" and integrated "Comfort with AI", "Perceived ease to use", and "Engagement in self-reflection" into "Confidence with AI"

citation: Kim Junhewk, Kim So Yeon, Jung Hoi-In, Kang Jeong-Hyun. (2026). A competency-based curriculum for geriatric dentistry in undergraduate and postgraduate education : a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09625-6
title: Eight thematic categories organize geriatric dentistry curriculum content: public health, aging changes, geriatrics/gerodontology, oral and maxillofacial alterations, pharmacy, dental practice, communication, and ethical/legal issues
description: The review's thematic synthesis produced eight major thematic categories spanning the knowledge, clinical skills, and professional attitudes required for care of older adults. The article states: "A comprehensive review identified eight major thematic categories relevant to geriatric dentistry curricula: (1) public health issues; (2) aging and age-related changes; (3) geriatrics and geriatric dentistry; (4) aging-related oral and maxillofacial alterations; (5) pharmacy; (6) dental practice; (7) communication; and (8) ethical and legal issues." These were later consolidated into six competency domains.

constraints: Overlapping or outdated topics were merged or refined to improve conceptual clarity, per the authors
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, clinical skills, and professional attitudes for geriatric oral health care
examples: Table 5 details subcategories such as dysphagia, polypharmacy, root caries, and decision-making capacity under the eight categories

citation: Saza Salas Laura Daniela, Hernandez Rincon July Andrea, Hernandez Rincon Erwin Hernando, Ulloa Rodriguez Mauricio Fernando, Diaz Quijano Diana Marcela, Jaimes Peñuela Claudia Liliana. title: Eight interrelated competency domains framework for family physicians in primary healthcare
description: The review proposes an integrated framework of eight competency domains for family physicians in PHC: communication, knowledge management, health promotion, information and communications technology, clinical and administrative management, community-oriented and public health-oriented care, teaching and research, and a cross-cutting competency focused on PHC. Each category is enriched by "a diverse set of interrelated components" listing specific skills, attitudes and knowledge (Table 4). constraints: No critical appraisal of internal or external validity of included studies was conducted

article_title: Geriatric core competencies for non-geriatricians and nurses: a scoping review.
citation: Yang Deng-Chi, Yu Yung-Chen, Lee Yi-Hsuan, Su Ruei-Ning, Lin Wei-Hung, Lai Pei-Chun. (2025). Geriatric core competencies for non-geriatricians and nurses: a scoping review. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-025-06806-8
title: Eighteen-domain integrated classification of geriatric core competencies
description: The review consolidates competencies from ten consensus studies into 18 distinct domains: basic, clinical, and social sciences of ageing, professionalism, communication, teamwork, disease and comorbidity, optimizing function, geriatric assessment, geriatric syndromes, pharmacologic/medication management, cognitive/dementia problems, falling and gait abnormalities, healthcare planning, palliative care, transitions of care, patient safety and quality care, and research. The authors state this "integrated domain-based classification" allowed them "to systematically organize and compare competencies across different sources." Pharmacologic/medication management and cognitive/dementia problems each appeared in seven of the ten studies.

constraints: The classification was applied to the ten included studies, mostly published before 2017 and mostly from American institutions

Studies were conducted mostly in Iran and European countries, with intervention-arm samples of 20 to 217.
requirements: Eligible studies had to be randomized or non-randomized controlled trials comparing e-learning against traditional lecture or no training
constraints: Unpublished grey literature and case reports/series were excluded

citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Eight practical considerations for designing and developing adaptive e-learning environments
description: Based on the review results, the authors present "eight practical considerations for the design and development of AEEs based on the results of this systematic review for educators and educational researchers" (Table 3): developing the educational content, selecting a theoretical framework, selecting the adaptivity method, selecting the adaptivity goal(s), selecting the adaptivity timing, selecting the adaptivity factor(s), selecting the adaptivity type(s), and determining technical resources and selecting the adaptive e-learning platform. constraints: The considerations are derived from a review of 21 studies in health professions education with generally high risk of bias and low-to-very-low quality of evidence
examples: The review's Table 3 lists the eight considerations with explanations, e.g. adaptivity goals may be to increase learning effectiveness, increase learning efficiency, modify behavioural predictors or improve cognitive/metacognitive processes

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges
citation: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105
title: Eight-category taxonomy of AI technologies in elementary STEM education
description: The review organizes the field into eight AI technology categories identified through preliminary scoping: intelligent tutoring systems and conversational AI, automated assessment and feedback, learning analytics and predictive modeling, computer vision for engagement monitoring, multimodal sensing and biometric analysis, adaptive content generation, educational robots and embodied AI, and extended reality with AI enhancement. target_learning_goals: STEM learning outcomes across science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, individually or integrated
examples: The review used the eight categories to code all 258 included studies and report category shares (45% tutoring/conversational AI down to 4% XR)

article_title: Teaching approaches and strategies that promote healthy eating in primary school children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Dudley, D. A., Cotton, W. G., & Peralta, L. R. (2015). Teaching approaches and strategies that promote healthy eating in primary school children: a systematic review and meta-analysis. constraints: Categorisation derived largely from Hattie's synthesis of meta-analyses; some studies included more than one strategy in their intervention group
target_learning_goals: Healthy eating behaviours: food consumption and energy intake, fruit and vegetable consumption or preference, reduced sugar consumption or preference, nutritional knowledge

citation: Chengere Ashebir Mekonnen, Bono Beyene Dobo, Zinabu Samuel Assefa, Jilo Kedir Woliy. (2025). Enhancing secondary school students’ science process skills through guided inquiry-based laboratory activities in biology. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320692
title: Eight-stage guided inquiry laboratory activity cycle structured into the 5E lesson format
description: The GIBLEI approach organizes each laboratory lesson as an eight-stage cycle: receiving semi-structured problems a week ahead, researching and planning experimental procedures, outlining experiments with hypotheses and variables, sharing designs with peers, conducting experiments and recording data, presenting conclusions linked to theory, answering follow-up questions, and assessment. Daily lesson plans were structured into the 5E format (engage, explore, explain, elaborate, evaluate), with most guided inquiry activities placed in the exploration phase.
requirements: Teacher and laboratory technician support at each stage, including provision of materials and facilitation of peer design discussions
constraints: Designed for Grade 10 biology unit topics; implemented over a complete unit spanning eight weeks
target_learning_goals: Hypothesis formulation, experimental design, data interpretation, and drawing conclusions
examples: Students received semi-structured problems a week before each class, then independently researched and planned experiments before conducting them in groups with teacher-provided materials.

article_title: Strategies and barriers to implementing physically active teaching in universities from the perspective of lecturers: a qualitative study.
citation: Rupp Robert, Wallmann-Sperlich Birgit, Bucksch Jens. (2025). Strategies and barriers to implementing physically active teaching in universities from the perspective of lecturers: a qualitative study. BMC Public Health 25, Article 855. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22075-x
title: Catalogue of 18 physically activating teaching methods for university courses
description: The study compiled 18 distinct teaching methods, derived from lecturers' own interview statements, that integrate learning processes with physical activity in a pedagogical-didactic manner. Examples include group work, gallery walk, jigsaw method, learning circuit, 4-corner-method, pair interview, and change of learning location. The article states: "All together, we identified 18 distinct teaching methods (e.g. group work, gallery walk) that integrate learning processes with physical activity in a pedagogical-didactic manner." Table 2 lists each method with its description and number of references.
requirements: Methods must synchronise physical activity with learning so that physically active time is also learning time pursuing pedagogical-didactic goals
constraints: Most methods were mentioned by only one to a maximum of two lecturers; group work is the only one implemented to a certain extent and frequency
target_learning_goals: student activation and learning-process support while interrupting sedentary behaviour
examples: Gallery walk: working groups display results in the classroom and all students walk around viewing other groups' results; pair interview: students walk around the classroom in pairs discussing a given question

article_title: Development and validation of a simulation-based assessment of operative competence for higher specialist trainees in general surgery.
citation: Toale Conor, Morris Marie, Roche Adam, Voborsky Miroslav, Traynor Oscar, Kavanagh Dara. (2024). Development and validation of a simulation-based assessment of operative competence for higher specialist trainees in general surgery. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11024-1
title: Pilot eight-station simulation-based assessment of operative competence for higher specialist general surgery trainees
description: A time-limited eight-station OSCE-style assessment built on the OSATS examination format, using bio-hybrid models (e.g. ileostomy reversal, emergency laparotomy) and LapSim virtual-reality stations (laparoscopic appendicectomy, cholecystectomy, right hemi-colectomy vessel ligation). Procedures were selected via a modified CAMES needs-assessment Delphi process. Performance was scored with an equally weighted modified Procedure-Based Assessment checklist plus OSATS tool, with a 30-min briefing and modified Angoff pre-assessment standard setting.
requirements: Examiners familiarized with format, tools, and models prior to the assessment
rater training conducted before the assessment
pre-assessment standard setting using a modified Angoff method
constraints: The article states pilot data with a limited number of trainee participants does not yet support implementation in informing high-stakes assessment outcomes
due to time and feasibility constraints, key component tasks rather than entire procedures were simulated at some stations
target_learners: higher specialist trainees (ST5–ST8) in general surgery
target_learning_goals: operative competence sufficient to operate safely as an independent practitioner in general surgery
examples: Thirteen candidates undertook the assessment across eight 15-min stations at the National Surgical Training Center, RCSI, scored by ten consultant-surgeon assessors

article_title: Emotional intelligence impact on academic achievement and psychological well-being among university students: the mediating role of positive psychological characteristics.
citation: Shengyao Ye, Xuefen Lin, Jenatabadi Hashem Salarzadeh, Samsudin Nadia, Chunchun Ke, Ishak Zahari. (2024). Emotional intelligence impact on academic achievement and psychological well-being among university students: the mediating role of positive psychological characteristics. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01886-4
title: Integrated emotional intelligence and positive psychology mediation framework
description: The article integrates Emotional Intelligence Theory with Positive Psychology Theory into one structural framework in which "emotional intelligence as the main independent variable, self-efficacy, motivation, and resilience as three mediators, and psychological well-being and academic achievement as two dependent variables". It explains how emotional abilities translate into outcomes: emotional skills raise self-efficacy, motivation, and resilience, which in turn raise well-being and achievement. The framework was tested with SEM on 518 Chinese university students and compared across educational levels.
requirements: Validated measurement scales for emotional intelligence (WLEIS), self-efficacy, motivation, resilience, and psychological well-being (Ryff's SPWB)
constraints: Tested among undergraduate and postgraduate students in China; academic achievement measured as self-reported GPA categories
examples: The study assessed emotional intelligence with the 16-item Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale and analysed the model separately for undergraduate (N = 323) and postgraduate (N = 189) groups.

article_title: Predicting student and instructor e-readiness and promoting e-learning success in online EFL class during the COVID-19 pandemic: A case from China.
citation: Yang Chunye, Xu Defeng. (2023). Predicting student and instructor e-readiness and promoting e-learning success in online EFL class during the COVID-19 pandemic: A case from China. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284334
title: Eight-category taxonomy of impediments to online EFL classes reported by students and instructors
description: The article organizes the challenges reported by both students and instructors into eight categories: "technical challenges, learning process, learning environments, self-control, health concern, learning materials, assignment, and learning effect and assessments". It adapts the taxonomy from Zou et al. and expands it with aspects drawn from its own questionnaire, presenting student-reported categories in Table 5 and instructor-reported categories in Table 6. The taxonomy is used to explain why e-readiness fell below the ready level in each phase.
requirements: Data on impediments collected from both students and instructors via open-ended questionnaire items
constraints: Derived from a single online EFL context in inland China during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: undergraduate EFL students in Chinese higher education
target_learning_goals: successful engagement and completion of online EFL courses
examples: Table 5 lists student-reported items such as payment, internet connectivity, weak and feeble signal, absent-minded, and poor eyesight; Table 6 lists instructor-reported items such as internet lag, student participation, and no proper assessing methods.
key_sources: Yang Chunye, Xu Defeng. (2023). Predicting student and instructor e-readiness and promoting e-learning success in online EFL class during the COVID-19 pandemic: A case from China. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284334

article_title: Exploring the structural relationships between medical students' motivational regulation, cognitive learning, and academic performance in online learning.
citation: Yun Heoncheol, Kim Seon, Chung Eun-Kyung. (2021). Exploring the structural relationships between medical students’ motivational regulation, cognitive learning, and academic performance in online learning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2021.193
title: Eight-strategy motivational regulation questionnaire (30 items, four constructs) adapted for medical students
description: A survey instrument adapted from the eight-MRS questionnaire extended by Schwinger and colleagues, measuring motivational regulation in medical students. "The MRS questionnaire consists of 30 items with four constructs: interest enhancement, goal orientation, behavioral reinforcement, and environmental control." Each item uses a 5-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, with higher scores indicating more active MRS use. The article used it as the exogenous measure in the SEM.
requirements: Validated by confirmatory factor analysis and correlation analysis with college student subjects, per the article
target_learning_goals: motivational regulation of learning effort and persistence in online learning
examples: Administered online in July 2020 to 510 students at a Korean public medical school after transition to partial online education

article_title: Simulation-based Education and Human Factors Training in Postgraduate Medical Education: A Northern Ireland Perspective.
citation: Lawson Sara, Reid James, Morrow Michael, Gardiner Keith. (2018). Simulation-based Education and Human Factors Training in Postgraduate Medical Education: A Northern Ireland Perspective. The Ulster Medical Journal 87(3):163-167. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6169420/
title: Eight design features for effective simulation as an educational tool
description: The article enumerates eight aspects shown to be important when using simulation as an educational tool: "curriculum integration, range of difficulty, being aware of multiple learning strategies i.e. different group sizes or with or without an instructor, clinical variation, a controlled safe learning environment, individualised learning, defined outcomes and validity". This list functions as a design checklist for simulation-based curricula alongside repetitive practice.
requirements: Simulation programmes should incorporate curriculum integration, defined outcomes and validity among the listed features
examples: The article presents the list as drawn from established best-evidence guidance on features and uses of high-fidelity medical simulations.

article_title: Acceptance of technology-enhanced learning for a theoretical radiological science course: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Nkenke Emeka, Vairaktaris Elefterios, Bauersachs Anne, Eitner Stephan, Budach Alexander, Knipfer Christoph, Stelzle Florian. (2012). Acceptance of technology-enhanced learning for a theoretical radiological science course: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-18
title: Eight-module radiological science e-learning course with weekly e-mail reminders, self-assessment questions and staffed online Q&A
description: The TEL condition was an online course on the Virtual University of Bavaria platform comprising "eight online modules" containing texts, images, graphs, videos, hyperlinks, reference lists and tests. Each module was planned for one week, opened with learning targets and initial multiple-choice self-assessment questions, ended with further questions with automated feedback, and was prompted by an invitation e-mail and a reminder after three days. Students could post questions on the Medlearn platform, answered by academic staff within 24 hours.
requirements: Students had to sign in to the e-learning platform to access the online content
An optional introductory session familiarized students with the platform to avoid non-users
constraints: During the course no questions were posted on the online platform, despite the possibility of contacting staff online at all times
target_learning_goals: theoretical radiological science: radiation physics, X-ray production and interactions, radiation dose, imaging equipment, radiation protection, image creation, normal radiological anatomy of teeth and jaws
examples: All 21 TEL students logged on to the platform; module use ranged from up to 60 minutes to over 600 minutes across students
